subject: Art & Design
title: CGI: From Jurassic Park to Everything
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on CGI: From Jurassic Park to Everything.

hook.text: When the T. Rex appeared in Jurassic Park (1993), audiences gasped. CGI dinosaurs looked completely real.

buildup.text: Computer-Generated Imagery (CGI) creates visual elements digitally that would be impossible or too dangerous to film.

discovery.text: Spielberg used CGI for only 6 minutes of Jurassic Park. The rest was practical effects and clever editing.

twist.text: Bad CGI ages terribly. Good CGI is invisible — you don't even realize you're looking at it.

climax.text: Films like Avatar and Planet of the Apes show CGI can create emotion, not just spectacle.

punchline.text: The best CGI is the CGI you don't notice.

quiz.question: How much CGI did Jurassic Park actually use for dinosaurs?
options: Only about 6 minutes — the rest was practical effects

details.summary: CGI transformed cinema after 'Jurassic Park' proved digital creatures could look photorealistic. Within a decade, films could create entire worlds, de-age actors, and populate battle scenes with digital armies. Today, even supposedly 'real' films use CGI to erase wires, extend sets, and alter skies.
details.whyItMatters: CGI removed cinema's physical limitations but created new questions about authenticity. When anything is possible, the challenge shifts from 'can we show it' to 'should we show it' — and audiences debate whether digital perfection sacrifices.
takeaways: Jurassic Park proved CGI creatures could be photorealistic
CGI now handles everything from entire worlds to sky replacement
Digital perfection raises questions about authenticity

faq.question: How much CGI is in a typical modern film?
faq.answer: Far more than audiences realize. Even dramas and comedies use CGI for sky replacement, set extension, crowd duplication, and removing unwanted elements. A Marvel film might have 2,500+ visual effects shots. Even 'realistic' films routinely contain hundreds of invisible CGI adjustments.

faq.question: Is CGI getting better or are audiences getting tired of it?
faq.answer: Both. Technology improves constantly, but audience fatigue with CGI-heavy spectacle is real. Films that blend practical and digital effects (like 'Dune' and 'Top Gun: Maverick') receive praise for their physicality, suggesting audiences value tangible reality even as digital tools advance.
